newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian dlr edges upward amid news barrage.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian dlr edges upward amid news barrage.

text.p: The Australian dollar edged higher through a jumpy session Tuesday as the market was bombarded with developments at home and abroad.

A surprisingly strong set of domestic retal sales data seemed to have substantially reduced the risk of a rate cut here, but that was countered by a report the Federal Reserve was thinking of hiking U.S. rates by as much as 0.5 point.

News the U.S. had launched air and missile attacks on Iraq briefly stirred dollar buying. Dealers said a rise in oil prices was supportive of the currency, but the crisis was simply not dangerous enough to prompt real safe haven demand.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had inched to US$0.7913/18 from an early US$0.7889/98 and US$0.7896/01 late Monday.

Dealers said taken overall the day's events favoured a higher dollar and looked for it to test US$0.7935 chart resistance offshore with a chance of seeing US$0.7960 if the Reserve Bank held its hand on rates.

The latter looked more likely after retail trade data today showed consumers went on a department store spending spree in July driving sales up a hefty 2.4 percent. That was the largest monthly rise since May 1994 and dwarfed market forecasts of a miserly 0.4 percent gain.

Dealers thought such a strong outcome, even if statistically suspicious, might sway the RBA board against sanctioning another easing at its monthly board meeting today, particularly as it was only a month since the last 0.5 point cut.
However, analysts cautioned that the bank always played down the importance of one month's data and, anyway, a recommendation on policy would have been made to the board last week.

"Despite the spike in July sales, the trend has continued to weaken and is consistent with economic growth easing back," said John Peters, a senior economist at Westpac. "We still see the RAB cutting by 0.50 point, but probably not at this meeting."
Dealers said if the RBA had decided to move the bank was most likely to announce the change during Wednesday's money market operations at 9.30 am (2330 GMT).

The debt market certainly seemed to have abandoned all hope of a near term rate cut with the September 90-day futures contract slid 13 basis points to 93.08 and the 10-year bond tumbled 0.180 point to 91.720.

The dollar relief was restrained by a report in the Wall Street Journal that the Federal Reserve was considering hiking its rates by 0.50 point if U.S. economic data show clear signs of slowing by its September 24 policy meeting.
The market had been leaning toward a tightening after a run of robust U.S. data recently, but had thought rates would only rise by 0.25 point.

A half point would sharply narrow the Australian dollar's yield premium over its U.S. counterpart, although analysts emphasised the differential against Japan was more important these days and that attraction showed no sign of fading.

There were rumours of buying for an A$ dual currency samurai bond this afternoon and talk a number of issues were lined up for this week. Japanese demand for these high yielding bonds has played a big part in the dollar's rise this year.
The U.S. strike on Iraq was seen supporting the dollar via higher oil prices. Oil is a major export earner for Australia and rising prices would also feed into higher commodity indices.
It rose to 86.48/58 yen from 86.20/30 -- Japan imports all its oil -- and to 58.1 in trade weighted terms from 57.9.

But dealers said the importance of such events tended to be overstated. "I can't see any lasting impact from the Middle East because the conflict won't last long," said Steve Shuster, forex head at Citibank. "Even if war breaks out we all know what the inevitable conclusion will be. The safe haven affect is much overrated." -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
